rv.q: Dustin Wills' subtle direction perfectly balances kitchen-sink realism with the bizarre elements creating an endearingly off-kilter, but ultimately healing family drama, unlike any other.

His inspired direction of Caswell’s play is a wild ride, and the play itself, “Wet Brain,” which had its world premiere Thursday at Playwrights Horizons Tuesday, gives this gifted director plenty of opportunities to go completely off the rails in a very good way.
Wet Brain , co-produced by Playwrights Horizons and MCC Theater, offers a gripping, grating look at alcoholism and its effects on loved ones.
He does it with robust assurance, charging his actors with a brand of electricity matching the explosive quality of Caswell's writing.
Director Dustin Wills has put together a production that allows us to go to a dubious Outer Space in order to contemplate these characters' credibly complicated inner space, and perhaps our own.
It is moments like this that prove that while Wet Brain might be an imperfect play, it has vital lessons to offer us and is a compelling portrait of dysfunction.
It's a shame the script isn't able to sustain the solid premise.
Near the end of the play, we enter one of Joe’s hallucinations in a stunning coup de theatre moment that is visually captivating but dramatically rather hollow.

cn.t: Critics praise this dysfunctional family drama for its genre-bending ambition and strong ensemble, though some feel its promising exploration of addiction and trauma deserves more room to breathe in its one-act format.
